# How to Edit Part of an Image with AI Without Changing the Rest

> **In short:** Modern AI image tools can edit just one part of a photo if you tell them clearly what to change AND what to keep the same. This guide walks you through a simple two-sentence prompt pattern that works in ChatGPT, Google Gemini, Adobe Firefly, and most other AI editors.

You snapped a great photo of your dog at the beach. The light is perfect, the composition is great, and your dog is doing something adorable. But there's a stranger in the background wearing a bright orange shirt, and it's pulling your eye away from everything you actually wanted to capture. You don't want to learn Photoshop. You just want that one person gone.

That's the kind of small edit people run into every day, and it's exactly what the latest AI image editors handle well — if you ask the right way.

The trick is a simple pattern: write one short instruction that does two jobs at once. It says what to change, and it says what to stay the same. Older AI image tools often ignored the second half. Newer ones are trained to pay close attention. Here's how to use that to your advantage.

## Before you start

You'll need:

- An AI tool that edits images. ChatGPT, Google Gemini, and Adobe Firefly all do this. Most work through a website or app — no special hardware needed.
- A photo you want to edit (JPG or PNG).
- A free or paid account, depending on the tool.

You don't need any design background. We'll cover each idea as we go.

## Step 1 — Open the tool and upload your image

Open the tool in your browser or app and log in. Look for a button labeled "upload," "attach," or sometimes a small picture icon. Tap it and choose the photo from your computer or phone.

> 💬 You don't need to type anything yet — just make sure your photo is loaded and visible on screen.

You'll know it worked when: you see your image as a thumbnail or in the chat area, and the text box is empty and ready for your instruction.

## Step 2 — Name the exact thing you want to change

Type the first half of your prompt: a clear, specific description of the one element you want to alter. Be precise — what it looks like, where it sits in the frame, and what should happen to it.

A few examples:

- "Remove the person in the orange shirt on the right side."
- "Change the gray car in the background to a red bicycle."
- "Make the small plant on the windowsill bigger and add more leaves."

Notice how each one names the object, its location, and the desired change. That's the change half of the pattern.

> 💬 Prompt example: "Remove the person in the orange shirt on the right side of the image."

You'll know it worked when: your sentence mentions exactly one element, in one place, with one desired change. If you find yourself saying "and also..." a lot, you're asking for too much at once.

## Step 3 — Add the "keep everything else" instruction

This is the part most people skip, and it's the part that does the most work. Right after your change request, add a sentence telling the AI what NOT to touch.

Use simple language like:

- "Keep the rest of the photo exactly the same."
- "Don't change the dog, the beach, the sky, or the lighting."
- "Preserve the background, the shadows, and the overall mood."

In AI circles, this is sometimes called "preservation prompting" — telling the model what to leave alone. The model is trained to listen to this second instruction as carefully as the first.

> 💬 Prompt example: "Remove the person in the orange shirt on the right side of the image. Keep everything else exactly the same — the dog, the beach, the lighting, the sky, and the colors."

You'll know it worked when: you can read your full prompt out loud and someone could point to which sentence is the change and which is the keep. If it's not obvious, rewrite it.

## Step 4 — Mention style, lighting, and mood if it matters

Sometimes the AI does the edit but shifts the lighting or color tone in a way that makes the change stand out. A short style note at the end of your prompt can prevent this.

Try adding one of these:

- "Match the same soft afternoon lighting."
- "Keep the photo's warm color palette."
- "Don't change the camera angle or the focus."

This isn't always necessary, but for subtle edits — removing a small object, fixing a smudge, swapping a sign — it's often the difference between a clean fix and one that looks obviously edited.

> 💬 Prompt example: "...Keep everything else exactly the same — the dog, the beach, the lighting, the sky, and the colors. Match the soft afternoon lighting and don't shift the color tone."

You'll know it worked when: your prompt reads like a complete sentence a real person would say, with both a request and a guardrail.

## Step 5 — Send it and look carefully at the result

Press send (or hit Enter, depending on the tool). The AI usually takes a few seconds. When it's done, you'll see a new version of your image.

Now look at it the way you'd look at a friend's photo before you say "looks good." Ask yourself:

- Did the thing I asked to change actually change?
- Did everything else stay the same?
- Are there any new weird artifacts — a smudge, a shadow that doesn't make sense, a blurry patch?

If something is off, don't start over. Just describe the new problem in your next message.

> 💬 Follow-up example: "Good, but the sky now looks slightly more blue than the original. Please match the original sky color more closely."

You'll know it worked when: your edit looks like it belongs in the original photo, not pasted on top of it.

## Step 6 — Iterate in small steps instead of starting over

This is the mindset shift that makes AI editing actually useful. Most people treat it like a one-shot task — type a prompt, hope for the best, give up. The people who get good results treat it like a conversation.

If the first result is close but not right, send a short follow-up describing only the remaining issue. Don't ask for the whole thing again. The AI remembers the image and your previous instructions for the rest of the chat session.

Good follow-ups look like this:

- "The shadow under the dog is gone — please put it back."
- "The red bicycle looks too big. Make it smaller, like the original car."
- "Almost perfect, but the wall behind looks slightly pinker than before."

> 💬 Follow-up example: "The dog now has slightly bluer fur than the original. Please match the original fur color exactly."

You'll know it worked when: each follow-up fixes one small thing without breaking the things you've already fixed.

## Common mistakes

- **Forgetting the "keep" half.** If you only say what to change, the AI will often tweak lighting, colors, or backgrounds too. Always add the second sentence.
- **Asking for too many edits at once.** "Remove the person, change the sky, add a dog, and make the sand pink" is too much. Break it into separate rounds.
- **Being vague about location.** "Change the thing on the left" is hard for the AI to follow. "Change the small red sign on the left side near the fence" works much better.
- **Giving up after one try.** The first attempt is rarely perfect. Small follow-up prompts usually get you there in two or three rounds.

## What this means for you

- **If you just want quick personal edits**: this pattern works for cleaning up vacation photos, removing strangers from group shots, or swapping a small object for something fun. You don't need any software beyond the AI tool itself.
- **If you run a small business or side project**: this is how you make clean product photos, mock up posters, or test visual ideas without paying for a designer. Be specific about brand colors and lighting, and you'll get usable results in minutes.
- **If you're new to AI tools in general**: this is one of the easiest places to start. Image editing is forgiving — small mistakes are obvious, so you learn fast. And the "say what to keep" trick transfers to writing, video, and other AI tools too.

## Wrap-up

The pattern is simple: name one thing to change, name everything else to keep, mention lighting if it matters, and iterate in small follow-ups. That's it. You don't need fancy software or design skills — just a clear sentence and a willingness to refine.

Try it tonight. Pick a photo on your phone, open your favorite AI tool, and run one edit using the two-sentence pattern. Once you see it work the first time, you'll start noticing small fixes everywhere.
